cim: AI-generated candidates in Pa. campaign ads spark debate over disclosure
cim_eredeti: AI-generated candidates in Pa. campaign ads spark debate over disclosure
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial intelligence has been used in ads in statewide, legislative, and congressional races in Pennsylvania, including digital representations of candidates saying words they did not actually say.

Artificial intelligence has been used in ads in statewide, legislative, and congressional races in Pennsylvania, including digital representations of candidates saying words they did not actually say.

Political ads have long featured attacks on candidates using look-alike actors, digital animation, and images edited or manipulated with programs like Photoshop.

But this year's campaign ads in Pennsylvania have featured likenesses of candidates generated with artificial intelligence---sometimes saying things they've never said.

The use of that technology in ads for statewide, congressional, and legislative races has sparked discussion---and scrutiny or criticism among some--- about the appropriateness of using generative A.I. in political ads and content.

"We're always deciding where to draw the line---that's part of the debate in a healthy democracy. But I do think that putting words into someone else's mouth is not necessarily protected speech," said Berwood Yost, director of Franklin and Marshall College's Center for Opinion Research.

Charles Palmer, executive director of Harrisburg University's Center for Advanced Entertainment & Learning Technologies, said that the use of generative A.I. by campaigns remains in the "Wild West" phase but that the "barn doors are open."

The inclusion of that content in political ads, Palmer said, falls in the same vein of campaigns using look-alike actors and photo or video editing to criticize or lampoon an opposing candidate.

"It really does sit in the same space. It's just evolved," he said. "The tools, the methods have gotten so much closer to the real world. Then again, it's hard for the average person to discern whether or not it's legitimate or true."

Among the ads getting significant playtime on television and digital advertising is an ad from Republican gubernatorial candidate Stacy Garrity that uses a digital facsimile of Gov. Josh Shapiro.

The rendering of Shapiro, which doesn't quite match his physical appearance or sound like him, references criticism and controversies raised by Garrity's campaign before disclosing around the 41-second mark that the ad is generated by artificial intelligence powered by data centers, highlighting a campaign attack against Shapiro's positions on data center development.

Then, green electricity shoots from Shapiro's hands, as if to hammer home the point that generative A.I. is being featured in the ad.

"We go to great lengths to disclose when A.I. is used," said Matt Beynon, a spokesperson for the Garrity campaign, who maintained that the claims in the ad are accurate.

Yost said the ads provide a way for Garrity to catch the attention of television viewers and those using video streaming services---especially after being significantly outraised in 2026 by Shapiro in campaign funding.

"It's probably far less expensive to create ads that way and if you're strapped for cash, you know, it certainly seems like a viable alternative," he said.

The Shapiro campaign was less than impressed with the ad.

“It’s unsurprising to see Donald Trump’s hand-picked candidate for Governor who supports aggressive data center deregulation trafficking in cheap, dishonest AI b***s**t," said Manuel Bonder, a spokesperson for the Shapiro campaign.

Pennsylvania lawmakers did pass a law signed by Shapiro this month that would require disclosure of AI content in advertising, though the law is focused on consumer goods and services. The law goes into effect in December.

But House lawmakers this year also unanimously passed legislation that would require disclosures in political ads and content that feature "deepfakes," or renderings meant to imitate politicians or candidates running for office. It also spells out penalties for misrepresentations of a candidate's positions or statements on an issue.

The legislation has not been voted on in the state Senate.

Rep. Tarik Khan, D-Philadelphia, a chief sponsor of the legislation, said the measure is needed in a time when artificially generated content in political advertising is becoming more sophisticated and commonplace.

"I think people should know that there should be consequences for what we're seeing," he said. "It's getting harder and harder to trust what you're seeing with your own eyes, and that's why we need to protect the public."
